knowledgePoint.zh: 为什么图像识别对计算机来说从根本上就是困难的
knowledgePoint.en: Why image recognition is fundamentally hard for computers

recallIntro.zh: 你闭上眼，思绪飘回那间挂满屏幕的教室。勒丘恩教授站在巨大的显示屏前，屏幕上正循环播放着各种图像——猫、汽车、手写数字。他看了你一眼，眼神里满是挑战的意味，仿佛在说：「你觉得让机器看见很简单？」
recallIntro.en: You close your eyes, and your thoughts drift back to that classroom lined with screens. Prof. LeCun stands before a massive display cycling through images — cats, cars, handwritten digits. He glances at you with a challenging look, as if saying: 「You think teaching machines to see is simple?」

recallOutro.zh: 你回过神来。像素与语义之间的巨大鸿沟仍在脑海中回响。机器看到的只是数字矩阵，而人类看到的是意义。这道鸿沟，究竟该如何跨越？
recallOutro.en: You return to the present. The vast chasm between pixels and semantics still echoes in your mind. Machines see only matrices of numbers, while humans see meaning. How can this chasm be crossed?

text.zh: 这间教室和你之前见过的都不一样。三面墙上都挂着大屏幕，播放着各种图像：人脸、风景、手写字母、工业零件。讲台上没有粉笔，只有一台连接着投影仪的工作站。门被推开，一位身材不高但精力充沛的中年人走了进来，深色卷发微微凌乱，眼神锐利而自信。他扫了一眼教室里的屏幕，满意地点了点头。
text.en: This classroom is unlike any you've seen before. Three walls are lined with large screens displaying all kinds of images: faces, landscapes, handwritten letters, industrial parts. There's no chalk at the lectern, just a workstation connected to a projector. The door opens and a compact but energetic middle-aged man walks in, his dark curly hair slightly tousled, his gaze sharp and confident. He glances at the screens around the room and nods with satisfaction.

text.zh: 欢迎来到我的课堂。我是勒丘恩，来自贝尔实验室，现在也在纽约大学任教。在我们开始讨论任何算法之前，我需要你们先理解一件事——视觉，是智能中最困难的问题之一。如果你想让机器理解世界，先教它用眼睛看。
text.en: Welcome to my class. I'm LeCun, from Bell Labs, and I also teach at NYU. Before we discuss any algorithms, I need you to understand one thing — vision is one of the hardest problems in intelligence. If you want machines to understand the world, first teach them to see with their eyes.

text.zh: 你们知道人类大脑皮层有多少面积用于视觉处理吗？大约百分之三十。三成！大自然用了几亿年的进化，把大脑最大的一块「地产」分配给了视觉。这说明什么？说明看见世界，理解看到的东西，是一项极其复杂的计算任务。
text.en: Do you know how much of the human cerebral cortex is devoted to visual processing? About thirty percent. Thirty! Nature spent hundreds of millions of years of evolution allocating the brain's largest piece of 「real estate」 to vision. What does that tell you? It tells you that seeing the world — understanding what you see — is an extraordinarily complex computational task.

text.zh: 让我给你们看一个简单的例子。（指向屏幕上一张猫的照片）你们看到了什么？一只猫，对吧？毫不费力。但计算机看到的是什么？它看到的是一个巨大的数字矩阵，比如说，一张224乘224的彩色图片，就是224乘224乘3，差不多15万个数字。对计算机来说，一只猫和一辆汽车之间的区别，就是15万个数字的不同排列。
text.en: Let me show you a simple example. (Points to a photo of a cat on the screen) What do you see? A cat, right? Effortless. But what does a computer see? It sees a massive matrix of numbers — say, a 224-by-224 color image means 224 times 224 times 3, roughly 150,000 numbers. To a computer, the difference between a cat and a car is just a different arrangement of 150,000 numbers.

text.zh: 这就是{计算机视觉}的核心难题，像素和语义之间存在巨大的鸿沟。像素告诉你每个点的亮度和颜色，但不告诉你「这是一只猫」。你需要从这些原始数字中，提炼出有意义的结构。从边缘，到纹理，到部件，到完整的物体——每一步都是一次抽象的飞跃。
text.en: This is the core challenge of {computer vision} — there is an enormous gap between pixels and semantics. Pixels tell you the brightness and color of each point, but they don't tell you 「this is a cat」. You need to distill meaningful structure from these raw numbers. From edges, to textures, to parts, to complete objects — each step is a leap of abstraction.

text.zh: 更糟糕的是，同一只猫可以有无数种样子。换个角度、换个光线、猫动一下尾巴，像素值就完全不同了。但你依然一眼就能认出它是同一只猫。你的大脑在做一件计算机极其困难的事情：从变化中提取不变的本质。
text.en: What makes it worse is that the same cat can look infinitely different. Change the angle, change the lighting, the cat flicks its tail — the pixel values are completely different. Yet you still recognize it as the same cat at a glance. Your brain is doing something extraordinarily difficult for computers: extracting invariant essence from variation.

text.zh: 从数学的角度来说，一张小小的图片就是一个极高维空间中的一个点。想象一下——15万维的空间！在这样的空间里，传统的统计方法根本没有用武之地。你需要的数据量会随着维度指数级增长，这就是所谓的「维度灾难」。你永远不可能收集到足够多的样本来覆盖这个空间。
text.en: From a mathematical standpoint, even a small image is a single point in an extremely high-dimensional space. Imagine — 150,000 dimensions! In such a space, traditional statistical methods are completely useless. The amount of data you need grows exponentially with the number of dimensions — this is the so-called 「curse of dimensionality」. You can never collect enough samples to cover this space.

text.zh: 面对图像识别的挑战，你觉得什么是最关键的困难？
text.en: Facing the challenge of image recognition, what do you think is the most critical difficulty?

text.zh: 像素和语义之间的鸿沟——原始数字和有意义的概念之间缺少桥梁
text.en: The gap between pixels and semantics — there's no bridge between raw numbers and meaningful concepts

text.zh: 说得好。这正是问题的本质。我们需要一种机制，能够自动地从像素中构建越来越抽象的表示——从边缘到形状，从形状到部件，从部件到物体。关键词是「自动」，因为我们不能指望人类去手动定义这些中间表示。
text.en: Well said. That's the essence of the problem. We need a mechanism that can automatically build increasingly abstract representations from pixels — from edges to shapes, from shapes to parts, from parts to objects. The key word is 「automatically, because we can't rely on humans to manually define these intermediate representations.

text.zh: 同一个物体的变化太多——角度、光线、遮挡都会让像素面目全非
text.en: Too much variation in the same object — angle, lighting, occlusion all change the pixels drastically

text.zh: 你抓住了视觉问题的一个核心痛点。一个好的视觉系统必须对这些变化保持不变性——不管猫是站着还是躺着，不管光线从左边来还是右边来，系统都应该说「这是猫」。我们需要的是一种能够忽略无关变化、保留本质特征的表示方法。
text.en: You've hit on a core pain point of the vision problem. A good vision system must maintain invariance to these variations — whether the cat is standing or lying down, whether the light comes from the left or right, the system should still say 「this is a cat」. What we need is a representation method that can ignore irrelevant variations while preserving essential features.

text.zh: 维度太高了——15万维空间中不可能用传统方法找到模式
text.en: The dimensionality is too high — it's impossible to find patterns in 150,000-dimensional space with traditional methods

text.zh: 数学直觉很敏锐。维度灾难确实是一个根本性障碍。但有趣的是，自然图像实际上只占据了高维空间中一个很小的子集——它们有结构，有规律。我们的任务就是找到能够利用这些结构的方法，从而把有效维度降低到可以处理的程度。
text.en: Sharp mathematical intuition. The curse of dimensionality is indeed a fundamental barrier. But interestingly, natural images actually occupy only a tiny subset of that high-dimensional space — they have structure, they have regularities. Our task is to find methods that exploit this structure, reducing the effective dimensionality to something manageable.

text.zh: 这些问题都是真实存在的。而在很长一段时间里，研究者们试图用手工方法来解决它们。
text.en: All of these problems are very real. And for a long time, researchers tried to solve them with handcrafted methods.

text.zh: 传统的方法是什么呢？{特征提取}。研究者花费大量时间，手工设计各种「特征检测器」：边缘检测器、角点检测器、纹理描述符……每一种特征都需要专家凭经验来设计，然后把这些特征喂给一个分类器。
text.en: What was the traditional approach? {Feature extraction}. Researchers spent enormous amounts of time handcrafting various 「feature detectors」: edge detectors, corner detectors, texture descriptors... Each type of feature had to be designed by experts based on experience, then these features were fed to a classifier.

text.zh: 这种方法有什么问题？首先，它依赖人类的聪明才智，你得提前知道什么特征是重要的。对于人脸识别，也许你可以设计出不错的特征。但换一个任务，比如识别医学影像中的肿瘤，你之前设计的所有特征可能就完全不适用了。每换一个问题，就得重新设计一套特征。
text.en: What's wrong with this approach? First, it depends on human ingenuity — you have to know in advance what features are important. For face recognition, maybe you can design decent features. But switch to a different task — say, identifying tumors in medical images — and all the features you designed before may be completely useless. Every new problem requires designing a whole new set of features.

text.zh: 我在法国读书的时候就觉得这条路走不通。（笑了笑）法国人嘛，天生有点叛逆。大家都在手工设计特征，我在想：为什么不让机器自己学会提取特征呢？如果我们足够聪明，应该能设计出一种学习算法，让它自动找到最有用的特征，而不需要人类逐个去发明。
text.en: When I was studying in France, I already felt this path was a dead end. (Smiles) We French are naturally a bit rebellious. Everyone was handcrafting features, and I was thinking: why not let the machine learn to extract features on its own? If we're clever enough, we should be able to design a learning algorithm that automatically finds the most useful features, without humans inventing them one by one.

text.zh: 这就是我一直坚持的理念：让机器「学会看」，而不是「告诉它怎么看」。特征应该从数据中自动学出来，而不是由人类预先定义。这个思路后来引导我走向了一种特殊的神经网络架构——但这是后面几节课的内容。
text.en: This is the idea I've always championed: let the machine 「learn to see」, rather than 「tell it how to see」. Features should be automatically learned from data, not predefined by humans. This line of thinking eventually led me to a special kind of neural network architecture — but that's for the coming lessons.

text.zh: 手工设计特征和让机器自动学习特征，你觉得哪种方式更有前途？为什么？
text.en: Between handcrafting features and letting machines learn features automatically, which approach do you think is more promising? Why?

text.zh: 自动学习更有前途——人类的直觉有限，机器可能发现我们想不到的特征
text.en: Automatic learning is more promising — human intuition is limited, machines might discover features we'd never think of

text.zh: 你说到我心坎里去了。这正是我二十多年来一直在做的事情。事实也证明了这一点——当我们最终让机器自己学习特征的时候，它学到的东西比人类设计的要好得多。有些特征甚至是人类从来没有想到过的，但它们确确实实有用。
text.en: You've spoken straight to my heart. This is exactly what I've been doing for over twenty years. And the facts have proven it — when we finally let machines learn features on their own, what they learned was far better than what humans designed. Some features were things humans had never even thought of, yet they genuinely worked.

text.zh: 手工设计更可靠——至少我们能理解每个特征的含义
text.en: Handcrafting is more reliable — at least we understand what each feature means

text.zh: 可解释性确实重要，我不否认。但「可靠」这个词需要重新定义。如果你的手工特征在一个数据集上效果很好，换一个数据集就崩溃了，那算可靠吗？学习型方法的优势在于适应性——给它新的数据，它就能学出新的特征。在我看来，这才是真正的可靠。
text.en: Interpretability is indeed important, I won't deny that. But the word 「reliable」 needs redefining. If your handcrafted features work great on one dataset but collapse on another, is that reliable? The advantage of learning-based methods is adaptability — give it new data and it learns new features. In my view, that's true reliability.

text.zh: 两者结合——用人类知识指导学习的方向
text.en: Combine both — use human knowledge to guide the direction of learning

text.zh: 有意思的想法。实际上，我设计的卷积神经网络就是某种程度上的「两者结合」——我们没有告诉网络具体要学什么特征，但我们设计了网络的结构，让它倾向于学习某些类型的特征。结构本身就是一种先验知识。这一点我们后面会详细讨论。
text.en: An interesting thought. In fact, the convolutional neural network I designed is to some extent a 「combination of both」 — we don't tell the network what specific features to learn, but we design the network's structure so it's inclined to learn certain types of features. The structure itself is a form of prior knowledge. We'll discuss this in detail later.

text.zh: 不管你持什么观点，有一个事实是不可否认的：到了2012年，自动学习特征的方法在ImageNet大规模图像识别竞赛中彻底击败了所有手工特征方法。差距之大，让整个计算机视觉社区震惊。但这是后面的故事，我们一步一步来。
text.en: Whatever your position, one fact is undeniable: by 2012, methods that automatically learn features completely crushed all handcrafted feature methods in the ImageNet large-scale image recognition competition. The margin was so large that it shocked the entire computer vision community. But that's a story for later — let's take it one step at a time.

suggestedContent.zh: 图像识别的核心难题：(1) 像素与语义之间的鸿沟；(2) 同一物体在不同角度、光线下像素完全不同；(3) 维度灾难——15万维空间中传统统计方法失效。手工特征依赖人类经验，不可扩展；自动学习特征才是更有前途的方向。
suggestedContent.en: Core challenges of image recognition: (1) the gap between pixels and semantics; (2) the same object looks completely different under different angles and lighting; (3) curse of dimensionality — traditional statistics fail in 150,000-dimensional space. Handcrafted features depend on human expertise and don't scale; automatically learned features are the more promising direction.

text.zh: 好消息是，大自然已经解决了这个问题——每个有眼睛的动物都在做视觉识别。下节课，我要带你们看看生物视觉系统是怎么工作的。两位神经科学家在1960年代做了一个精彩的实验，他们发现猫的视觉皮层有一种特殊的组织方式。这个发现，直接启发了卷积神经网络的诞生。
text.en: The good news is that nature has already solved this problem — every animal with eyes performs visual recognition. Next lesson, I'll show you how the biological visual system works. Two neuroscientists in the 1960s conducted a brilliant experiment and discovered that the cat's visual cortex has a special organizational pattern. This discovery directly inspired the birth of convolutional neural networks.

text.zh: 今天我想让你们记住一点：视觉看起来简单，是因为你的大脑太擅长了，以至于你感觉不到它在做什么。但当你试图让机器做同样的事情时，你才会意识到这项任务有多么复杂。尊重这个难度，才是解决它的第一步。
text.en: Here's what I want you to remember today: vision seems simple because your brain is so good at it that you don't notice what it's doing. But when you try to make a machine do the same thing, you realize just how complex this task is. Respecting this difficulty is the first step toward solving it.

suggestedContent.zh: 勒丘恩的核心理念：让机器「学会看」，而非「告诉它怎么看」。特征应从数据中自动学习，而非由人类手工设计。这种思路最终催生了卷积神经网络。
suggestedContent.en: LeCun's core philosophy: let the machine 「learn to see」, not 「tell it how to see」. Features should be automatically learned from data, not handcrafted by humans. This thinking ultimately gave rise to convolutional neural networks.

text.zh: 勒丘恩教授关掉了屏幕上循环播放的图像，拿起桌上的咖啡杯喝了一口。「回去想想，为什么你的大脑能毫不费力地认出一只猫，而最聪明的程序员写几万行代码也做不到这件事。想通了这一点，你就会理解我为什么选择了这条路。」他抬手挥了挥，大步走出了教室。
text.en: Prof. LeCun switches off the cycling images on the screens and takes a sip from his coffee cup. 「Think about why your brain can effortlessly recognize a cat while the smartest programmer can't do it with tens of thousands of lines of code. Once you understand that, you'll understand why I chose this path」. He waves his hand and strides out of the classroom.
